content: Diagnostic confirmation is considered the gold standard for identifying rabies cases in both humans and animals. However, in human cases, clinical diagnoses can also be confirmed through verbal autopsy, as outlined in Annex 11. For animals, particularly dogs, cases can be confirmed by evaluating them against established case definitions and using the investigation form provided in Annex 12. Active surveillance of healthy animals that have not been reported as being involved in human exposures is generally of limited value. This is because identifying a single rabies case often requires testing a large number of animals, which is resource-intensive and inefficient. Professionals such as private and public veterinarians, veterinary paraprofessionals, animal control officers, and game wardens are the most likely to encounter clinically rabid animals in their professional settings. These individuals are also typically the first to identify rabies cases at the community level and are integral to animal rabies surveillance efforts. They must be well-versed in recognizing clinical signs of rabies, collecting appropriate samples, and following the correct reporting procedures. When a person is bitten by a suspected rabid animal, all components of the surveillance and response system intersect. Integrated bite case management involves investigating suspected rabid animals and sharing information with both animal and human health investigators to conduct appropriate risk assessments. Although resource-intensive, such programs are crucial for preventing human deaths from rabies, particularly in areas where dog-mediated rabies is endemic. These programs also enhance the overall quality of rabies surveillance. Bite incidents should prompt immediate triage, including determining the vaccination status of the biting animal and conducting follow-up investigations if rabies is suspected. This may involve observing the animal for 10 days (in the case of dogs and cats) or performing post-mortem testing. Timely responses by medical and veterinary staff in the field are essential for ensuring proper case management and follow-up, improving case detection rates, and encouraging continued reporting by field and hospital staff. Feedback on reports, diagnostic test results, and guidance on case management and rabies control measures should be provided promptly. In countries with well-established rabies control programs, integrated bite case management can lead to more targeted use of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) based on risk assessments and diagnostic input. This approach reduces unnecessary PEP administration for low-risk exposures. Routine reporting and epidemiological analysis of surveillance data are essential for estimating trends and spatial dynamics of rabies cases. Understanding trends by species, including humans, forms the foundation for intervention programs. Basic trends should be estimated for the number of investigations and cases, including human PEP, rabid humans, and rabid animals. Surveillance data should be mapped to identify the distribution of cases and any gaps in surveillance coverage that may account for unobserved cases. Detailed reports should include control activities and their impact on the rabies burden. The surveillance system must be routinely monitored and evaluated to ensure that its objectives are being met and to improve its overall performance. This includes assessing the timeliness and completeness of monthly reporting and addressing deficiencies to ensure accurate and prompt annual analysis. Periodic evaluations, conducted every few years or when objectives change, are necessary to ensure the system operates efficiently and delivers high-quality data for public health interventions. Routine characterization of virus isolates from human and animal cases is encouraged, particularly in areas aiming for rabies elimination. This helps identify sources of infection and their geographical origins. Even after elimination, human and animal surveillance should continue, with viral characterization documenting any importation of rabies or unrecognized domestic circulation. Globally, harmonized processes are required to measure and acknowledge country progress toward the goal of zero human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030. Countries are categorized into phases of rabies elimination, ranging from endemicity to elimination and maintenance of freedom from disease. Achieving zero human deaths is defined as the absence of human deaths from dog-mediated rabies for at least 24 months in a country with adequate surveillance and effective rabies control programs. Validation of zero human deaths or interruption of rabies transmission requires robust evidence and data that can be independently assessed. Premature cessation of control measures could lead to disease resurgence with significant public health, economic, and political consequences. Core requirements for validation include mandatory notification of rabies in all species, continuous and effective surveillance meeting WHO and OIE standards, targeted sampling of susceptible animal species, and a national rabies control strategy involving mass dog vaccination and access to human PEP. Countries achieving zero human deaths or interrupting rabies transmission must demonstrate the absence of indigenous cases for at least 24 months, supported by molecular characterization and epidemiological investigations. Imported cases do not affect a country's status if the virus source is confirmed as non-indigenous and no secondary infections are detected.
